theme: Social justice; the wall completed; the exiles registered
readingInstruction: Read Nehemiah 5:1-7:73. A crisis arises inside the community, and Nehemiah rebukes the wealthy for exploiting the poor. Then the enemies change tactics. The wall is finished in fifty-two days.
settingTheScene: While the wall is rising, a cry goes up from the poor. Famine, taxes, and debt have driven them to mortgage their fields and sell their children into slavery to their own countrymen. This is a problem more dangerous than any external enemy. Nehemiah also faces personal schemes to distract and frighten him, but the wall is finished in the month of Elul.
observation: “There was a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers” (5:1).
“I was very angry when I heard their outcry” (5:6).
“I consulted with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles” (5:7).
“The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God?” (5:9).
“Out of reverence for God I did not do so” (5:15).
“Come and let us meet together… But they intended to do me harm” (6:2).
“I am doing a great work and I cannot come down” (6:3).
“So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days” (6:15).
interpretation:
The hardest challenge to the wall came from within. The poor were crushed by debt, and some of the rich were profiting from their brothers’ misery. This was exactly what the law of Moses forbade (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:35-37). Nehemiah is furious, yet notice what he does: he “consulted with myself,” meaning he took time to think before he acted. Then he called a great assembly and made his case on the basis of the fear of God and the witness to the nations. The nobles repent and give back the fields and interest. Nehemiah then points to his own example. As governor, he refused the food allowance due to him, because “the service was too heavy on the people.” He led with his own life.

Then the enemy changes tactics. Four times they invite him to a meeting, planning to harm him. Nehemiah’s answer is a classic: “I am doing a great work and I cannot come down.” He knew his calling and would not be pulled off it. The enemy tries a false accusation, then a hired prophet who tries to scare him into hiding in the temple. Nehemiah sees through it: “Should such a man as I run away?” He discerned that the prophet was bribed. Then he prays: “Now, O God, strengthen my hands.”

And the wall is finished in fifty-two days. Even the enemies recognize “this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.” But the end of chapter 6 shows that trouble remains: Tobiah keeps sending letters. Chapter 7 sets up the next task, which is to repopulate the city and put people back in order.
connection: James 5:1-6 condemns those who defraud their workers. Luke 3:11 and Acts 4:34-35 describe sharing with those in need. 1 Peter 5:2-3 calls leaders to serve as examples. Luke 9:51 says Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem. Philippians 3:13-14: “one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind… I press on.” Galatians 6:2: bear one another’s burdens.
application:
Ask whether there is anyone you could help who is burdened by debt or need. Act on it.

Think of your “great work.” What distractions do you need to say “I cannot come down” to?

Lead by example in one area where others look to you.
prayerPrompts: Ask God for the fear of him that treats others justly.
Ask him to keep you from taking advantage of the poor.
Thank him for the finished work.
